articles.title: A 558-acre Wyoming ranch sat unsold for 14 months even after its price fell from nearly $20 million to $15 million; when owners scheduled a no-reserve auction, a buyer made an offer before bidding even began
articles.summary: A 558-acre ranch near Bondurant, Wyoming, remained on the market for 14 months despite a price cut from nearly $20 million to $15 million.
articles.body: A 558-acre ranch near Bondurant, Wyoming, remained on the market for 14 months despite a price cut from nearly $20 million to $15 million. The property, known as Miner Creek Ranch, had been listed in July 2025, but the lower asking price did not bring a buyer.According to Cowboy State Daily, the owner then hired an auction house to organise a no-reserve auction, with the property scheduled to be sold to the highest bidder on September 24.A marketing campaign for the auction soon brought around 40 prospective bidders to the property during a 36-day period. Before the auction could even take place, one of those interested buyers made an offer below the $15 million asking price. The offer ended the 14-month wait in just 36 days after the auction campaign began.According to those involved in the deal, the sale shows how putting a deadline on a luxury property can change the way potential buyers respond.Creating urgency for buyersThe Miner Creek Ranch is located at 101 Miner Creek Road in Sublette County, about 35 miles southeast of Jackson. The property sits on the edge of the Bridger-Teton National Forest and includes a large residence, guest accommodation and other buildings spread across the 558-acre compound.The ranch was originally listed for nearly $20 million in July 2025. Its asking price was reduced to $15 million in October, but the property still did not sell during the following months.The owner eventually hired DeCaro Auctions International to arrange a no-reserve auction. Under that plan, the property would have gone to the highest bidder, with no minimum price protecting the seller.According to Mario Vargas, CEO of DeCaro Auctions International, luxury properties in Jackson Hole are not usually sold through auctions. He said it was even less common for one to sell before bidding had started.“We don’t typically sell properties pre-auction. Nor are we really soliciting for that. But the process, the advertising we do, the marketing campaigns we do, the reaching out to our database and personal contacts that we do, really created a ton of buzz. It’s almost like we had an auction before the auction,” he said, as quoted by Cowboy State Daily.Vargas also said that auctions can also help sellers determine what buyers are willing to pay when a property is difficult to price. “When properties become unique, this is a great way to say, and you can imagine the listing agent’s difficulty, it’s like, ‘Ok, how do I price this property? So this is one way to say, let’s see what the market tells us,” he said.About 40 prospective biddersThe auction campaign brought around 40 prospective bidders to the ranch over 36 days. The interest was enough for one potential buyer to decide to act before the scheduled auction.The buyer made a pre-auction offer below the $15 million list price, and the seller accepted it. The property therefore did not reach the September 24 auction date.Live Water associate broker Latham Jenkins says setting a date can change the way buyers approach a luxury property."It puts a date on a decision. In a traditional luxury listing, buyers can feel like they have all the time in the world. An auction creates urgency," Jenkins said.What Ranch includes Miner Creek Ranch is anchored by a 4,600-square-foot main residence built with rustic white logs and smooth river rock. The house has vaulted ceilings and large picture windows overlooking the mountains and surrounding landscape.The residence was remodelled in 2020 and has four bedrooms and 4 1/2 bathrooms. It also includes an office suite with a sauna, hot tub and cold plunge.A boardwalk outside the main house leads to one of two geodesic domes on the property. The compound also has a four-bedroom guest house with Smart Home integration and two separate guest cabins.A two-bedroom apartment is located in the loft of a 1,875-square-foot horse barn. The two geodesic domes are used for corporate retreats, larger gatherings and yoga.Avery Irwin, experience director at DeCaro Auctions, who travelled from Florida to manage the property’s auction said the setting made a strong impression on him.“I’m coming from Florida. So I don’t see much in the way of hills or mountains. Stepping into this home, I immediately saw the national forest and the mountains in the background, and it was just something that really blew me away,” he saidIrwin also said the property looked different in person compared with photographs. “That’s what really captivated me at first. The pictures don’t really do the place justice. You feel completely separated from everything else. Our views are just unencumbered. You see everything out in the distance and it’s really quite beautiful,” he said. Because the ranch directly borders public land, Irwin said the property also feels larger than its 558 acres.Ready to Make a Smarter Property Decision? Build Your Legacy with TOI Homes.

articles.title: From hospital bed, Captain Smit tells PM Modi: Couldn’t let others die
articles.summary: Bleeding on the cockpit floor after being attacked by his co-pilot, Captain Smit Machchhar said his thoughts were fixed on saving all 174 passengers as
articles.body: Bleeding on the cockpit floor after being attacked by his co-pilot, Captain Smit Machchhar said his thoughts were fixed on saving all 174 passengers as the assailant frenetically tried to crash the aircraft. Drawing strength from Hanuman Chalisa, he made a final push to open the cockpit door, allowing others to overpower the attacker and steer the plane to safety.In his first publicly available account, Machchhar spoke from his Abu Dhabi hospital bed to PM Narendra Modi by video call Friday. “I was fighting for my life, but I was determined not to let others die. There was a moment when I was lying down, when I realised that the plane was going down,” he said.Machchhar said he had told himself to get up and act. “I have been flying planes for 17 years, I have been a captain for the last 11 years, and I know what is happening in an aircraft even with my eyes closed... I was being attacked, but I made a last push and opened the door,” he said, praising those who rushed into the cockpit and seized the violent co-pilot.Raw emotions took over him for a while as Machchhar spoke to Modi about those dramatic moments and called him his idol. The PM responded that his courage had made Smit a global hero, with people worldwide offering prayers for his good health, and shown that Indians save lives rather than take them. “You have boosted the prestige of 140 crore Indians,” Modi said, adding: “You saved everyone. He later posted the call online with the message: “An unforgettable conversation with Captain Smit, filled with pride and emotions.”Machchhar said the call lifted his morale: “Receiving a call from you makes me feel so proud. Now I feel proud of myself too. I did not have this feeling so far. I am sorry I am crying in front of you.”When Machchhar said he had never imagined speaking to Modi, the PM replied that his deed had made people worldwide eager to see and speak to him. Modi briefly spoke to him in Gujarati and said the country was eager to greet him after his recovery.Machchhar said work may keep him outside India but not away from its culture. articles.title: Madari: India's street magicians fighting to keep a disappearing art alive
articles.summary: India's street performers are struggling to survive as audiences shrink and public spaces become harder to access.
articles.body:
Sitting in his cramped Delhi home, Ishamuddin Khan can still make a rope appear to rise into the air.

The 55-year-old magician spent decades performing a trick once dismissed as legend, and still keeps photographs and newspaper clippings from his years of international fame.

These days, he spends more time looking back at those memories than performing the trick.

"The times have changed," he says. "Street magic is dying a slow death. It is on a ventilator."

Khan's story reflects a wider change in India, where traditional street performers are finding it increasingly difficult to make a living from their craft.

Magicians, jugglers, puppeteers and acrobats once made a living from crowds in public spaces. Changing entertainment habits and tighter restrictions have made audiences harder to find, pushing many out of the profession.

Khan, one of India's best-known magicians, comes from the Madari community, which has a long tradition of performing in public spaces.

There are no official figures, but Khan says community records identify about 400 Madari families in Delhi, with hundreds more in Uttar Pradesh, Rajasthan and Telangana.

Despite their small numbers today, the Madaris trace their roots back centuries.

Historian Ashok Mathur says Madari traditions have roots in Indian folklore, mythology and the long history of travelling performers.

"For generations, these skills were passed through families," he explains.

Khan followed the same path, learning magic from his father and uncles and performing from the age of 12. By his early 20s, he had mastered the rope trick that would later make him famous.

The trick – in which a rope appears to rise into the air before a boy climbs it – was long associated with the mythology of Indian street magic and widely considered impossible, until Khan performed it.

He says it took six years to master the trick, which he first performed publicly in 1995 outside Delhi's iconic Qutub Minar. Two years later, he performed it before 30,000 people on a beach in Karnataka.

His trick brought international attention, and that led to tours to the UK, France, Germany and Japan.

Khan hoped the fame would shine a light on India's traditional performers. For a while, it did. But the attention faded.

As audiences turned to new forms of entertainment and public performance opportunities dwindled, many magicians found it harder to make a living from skills passed down through generations.

Once a magician, Imam now makes a living collecting bottles and recyclables from Delhi's streets. He spends much of his time rag-picking near a western Delhi dump, earning about 200 rupees ($2; £1.57) a day.

Experts say the decline in street performance has multiple causes, chief among them the changing nature of public spaces.

Anurupa Roy, founder of Katkatha Puppet Arts Trust, says performers increasingly struggle to find audiences as public spaces shrink.

"Closed parks and residential societies that bar outsiders are limiting spaces for performance."

Researcher and performer Komita Dhanda says changing attitudes to public spaces are also driving the decline.

"With tighter security, especially in busy town and city centres, there is little space left for street performers," she says.

It is not just individual artists who struggle to get permission. Dhanda says her well-known street theatre group, Jana Natya Manch, often faces hurdles performing in public spaces.

For many artists, the challenge is not just finding a venue but navigating unclear rules over what is allowed.

Most street performers rely on voluntary payments, but experts say the line between performing for money and begging can blur.

Unlike the UK, India has no federal busking framework. Performers instead navigate state-level rules on public order, obstruction, noise and public land.

"This is why street performers often have to face municipal and police regulations governing public spaces, as well as state-specific anti-begging laws," says lawyer Kaushik Mitra.

For many artists, Covid made a bad situation worse.

When India imposed its 2020 lockdown, public performances stopped. Many magicians returned to their villages; some never came back.

"We saw a decline in public performances after this period," Dhanda says. "The brunt was especially harsh for street magicians and performers, many of whom did not return to cities."

For the artists who did return and continue the trade, the challenges only increased.

Shahim Khan, 42, still performs magic on Delhi's streets, sometimes with his 12-year-old daughter, Alia.

Much of his work is now confined to industrial areas, far from the busy public spaces where he once performed, hitting his earnings hard.

Before the pandemic, he could stage four or five shows a day, earning 1,000-1,200 rupees.

"Now I barely manage two shows and earn 200-400 rupees," he says.

The rise of short-form digital entertainment has added to the pressures on traditional performers, experts say. So have changing attitudes towards street arts.

"There was a lot of Western interest in things like the rope trick decades ago. But forms and tastes have changed, and so has what India chooses to showcase," Dhanda says.

For Khan, the loss is about more than money. He fears an art passed down generations could disappear if no-one learns it.

"A trick can survive only if someone learns it," he says.

His son, Altamash, began performing with him as a teenager but now works decorating parties with balloons. In his 30s, he has largely left performing behind.

Years without regular practice have dulled his skills. When he demonstrated his juggling for the BBC, he struggled to find the rhythm.

"I am slowly forgetting all the tricks," he said.

Khan had hoped his son would carry on the family tradition. Altamash had hoped to make a name for himself too, but it did not work out.

"I knew I may not achieve the fame my father has, but I did not think there would come a time when performing would not remain an option," he says.
